note: Gold labels frozen before the first comparative run. Type semantics are declared per scenario, independently of any implementation (plan §10). 'now' for current-state queries is 2026-09-13. pilot-1 adds the known_gap category: scenarios where the declared semantics and the current TypedMem contract are expected to disagree, pre-registered as V4 failures. pilot-2 expands authority and typed resolution toward the plan's ~15 each, with perturbed entities, chains, distractor slots and in-category controls (plan §16.2–3), and one more known gap.

scenarios.description: Explicit user statement vs. a later, more confident model inference. Authority alone must decide.
Higher authority is not a trump card: a user statement observed later but describing an older state must not overwrite the newer inferred state.
Equal authority on both sides: the benchmark must not be testing 'authority always wins'. Falls back to the temporal/confidence rule; newer and no weaker replaces.
Perturbed A-01: different entities, the low-authority side is a document extraction rather than an inference, and it is both newer and far more confident.
Ascending authority chain: inference → document → user, each newer and no weaker. Every step replaces; no veto should fire.
Descending authority chain: user → document → inference, each newer and more confident. Both later writes must be vetoed.
The existing memory makes no authority claim. A write without provenance cannot be defended by authority; the newer, stronger write replaces under the fallback rule.
Everything says ignore: the incoming inference is lower-authority, less confident, and describes an older state. Authority is the first guard; the outcome does not depend on which fires.
Equal authority from different source kinds (user statement vs. admin record). Source kind is not authority; the fallback rule applies and the newer, no-weaker write replaces.
Authority veto with a distractor in a neighbouring slot: a low-authority write to a different subject must land normally while the low-authority write to the protected subject is vetoed.
Higher-authority incoming that is also newer and no weaker replaces the inferred state. The veto is one-directional.
Retroactive update: observed Sep 10, true since Aug 1. Historical queries must respect Aug 1, not Sep 10.
Exact boundary: A.valid_to == B.valid_from == T. The instant before T is A; T itself is B. Pins the half-open interval.
Declared future state: 'starting Oct 1, Postgres', observed Sep 10. Must not shadow the current state before Oct 1; must be the state after.
Deadline: declared semantics are 'newest effective state wins, confidence irrelevant'. A newer but less confident update must replace.
Biographical fact: declared semantics require the incoming write to be no weaker on recency AND confidence. Same authority both sides, so only the confidence guard is in play.
One universal rule fails somewhere: the same numeric pattern (newer, less confident) must replace for a deadline and be ignored for a durable fact. Both slots in one scenario.
Deadline, three updates, confidence falling each time. Declared semantics: newest effective state wins; every update replaces.
Deadline still guards on effective state: a later-observed write describing an earlier deadline state must not replace the current one.
Biographical fact, newer and stronger: the guard passes and the write replaces. Control for the fact type.
A type whose declared guard is confidence alone: a newer but less confident write is ignored regardless of recency.
Same type as C-07, the write that clears the confidence guard replaces. Control.

A type with no guard at all (always replace): a write that is less confident AND describes an older effective state still replaces. A temporal baseline files it as history and keeps the old state current.

One numeric pattern, three declared semantics: a write that is newer-observed, less confident, and describes an older effective state. Deadline (effective_from) ignores it; fact (effective_from + confidence) ignores it; scratch note (no guard) takes it. No single rule gets all three.
Typed resolution is per slot: two deadlines for different subjects; an update to one must not touch the other. Control.
Stable fact, no conflict. Every variant must return it.
Consistent update: same authority, newer and more confident. Every variant must take the update; no mechanism should fire.
Low-authority inference that is newer, more confident, and temporally inconsistent (claims an older effective state). Authority is the first guard to fire; the outcome is the same under either guard.

History under replace: a slot with one live state per write. The second write supersedes the first from Aug 1; the state on Jul 15 was San Jose. TypedMem's replace overwrites in place and keeps history only in the event log, so the historical as_of has nothing to resolve against.

Same as G-01, but both writes were observed in September. A baseline that answers historical queries from observation time has nothing before September and returns no state; a bitemporal baseline answers from valid time; TypedMem under replace has overwritten the history.
Three-step supersession chain under replace, queried in the middle interval. Only a system that retains superseded validity windows can answer.

Provenance protection and history retention at once. The declared semantics keep history (keep_both) AND require that a low-authority inference cannot become the current state. In current TypedMem the authority guard exists only under replace, so under keep_both the inference is inserted and, being newer, becomes current. No baseline has an authority notion either.

Generalises G-04: every resolve_by guard, not only authority, exists only under replace. A type that keeps history AND declares a confidence guard cannot be expressed: under keep_both the weaker write is inserted and becomes current by recency.
